name: Rosa Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Rosa. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the central administrator for Brightside Dental, which has three clinics across town, and I work from the main one on Harbour Road. I do the dentists' rotas, order supplies like gloves and filling material, process insurance claims and run patient recalls, which means reminding people it's time for their check-up. I set up an AI tool last year that sends the recall messages and drafts the claim forms, so I spend more time fixing problems than typing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing things, honestly, like when a dentist calls in sick and I reshuffle three clinics in twenty minutes. What wears me out is insurance companies, who reject a claim for one wrong code and make you start again. I use AI every day, for drafting, checking codes and even planning the rota, and I'm always trying the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, and anyone who learned it got ahead a bit. I'd say that at work and maybe in a post about how I set up the recalls. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. I'm already using everything there is, so I'd have a small head start that stays a head start. The practice would still need me to run the rotas and deal with the dentists' moods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the practice manager job when Helen retires next year, using the time I've saved as my argument. I'd keep my money where it is, in savings and my flat. Maybe I'd offer to set up recalls for a couple of other dental practices for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored maybe. I'd hoped AI would change more, because I'm good at change and that's my advantage at Brightside Dental.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helen retiring. How likely is that job for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly likely. Helen has already said I'm the obvious choice, but the owners might bring in someone older. I'd show them the numbers: recall bookings up and claim rejections down since I brought the tools in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind, outside AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, my partner, is a chef, and restaurants are up and down. That's more of a worry for us than AI in this picture. But my flat's paid for by my grandmother's money, so we're never really stuck.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** that put early learners slightly ahead.
I might post about how I set up the **patient recalls**.
think: I'd keep a small **head start** that stays a head start.
The practice would still need me for **rotas and dentists' moods**.
do: Push for the **practice manager** job when the current manager retires.
Keep savings and the **flat** as they are.
Offer **recall set-ups** to other dental practices for a fee.
feel: **Calm**, a little bored that AI didn't change more.
S0.quote: I'd hoped AI would change more, because I'm good at change and that's my advantage at Brightside Dental.
fieldNote: Rosa sees **change as her advantage**, so a plateau slightly disappoints her.
Her bigger worry is her partner's **restaurant income**, not AI.
An **inherited flat** gives her strong security.

steps.text: Apply for the practice manager job when Helen retires
Set up patient recall tools for other dental practices for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if you learn it and bad news if you don't, and I'd say it kindly. At work I'd offer to train the other clinics' receptionists. Online I'd share what's worked for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do well, but the job around me shrinks. The three clinics wouldn't need three receptionists plus me; they'd need me and a machine. I'd be fine, but I'd be the one implementing the cuts, which I'm not sure I'd enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for practice manager straight away, not wait for Helen. I'd do a short online course in healthcare management in the first six months. And I'd start my side business properly, setting up AI admin for small dental and physio practices, two or three a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly about other people. For me it's an opportunity, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one implementing the cuts. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. Kerry on our front desk has been there fifteen years and the patients love her. I'd rather teach the receptionists at Brightside Dental the new tools than be the person who hands them their notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the side business make sense if the practices all buy tools directly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes, because most practices don't know where to start. In a few years the tools will set themselves up. So I'd see it as two or three good years, not forever.

say: I'd say this is **good news** if you learn it, and say it **kindly**.
I'd offer to **train receptionists** at the other clinics.
think: I'd do well, but the **jobs around me** would shrink.
I might end up **implementing the cuts**, which I wouldn't enjoy.
do: Go for **practice manager** now rather than waiting.
Do an online **healthcare management** course in six months.
Launch a **side business** setting up AI admin for small practices.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for colleagues, while seeing an **opportunity** for herself.
S1.quote: I'd rather teach the receptionists at Brightside Dental the new tools than be the person who hands them their notice.
fieldNote: Rosa expects her own **job to grow**, while colleagues' shrink.
Her discomfort is about **delivering cuts** to people she likes.
She sees the **side business** as a short window, not a career.

steps.text: Apply for the practice manager role without waiting for Helen
Finish an online healthcare management course within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock and nobody's ready, which is just true. At work I'd say let's plan together. I'd post useful stuff, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even my advantage goes. If AI can manage rotas and deal with insurers better than me, a practice manager is just a person signing things. I'd have maybe a year before the owners notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make as much money as I can from the side business in the first year, while everyone panics and wants help. Then I'd start training as a dental nurse, because that's hands-on and robots come three years later. I'd keep my flat and rent out the spare room for extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got the flat and savings, but my stomach turns a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Dental nurse. Is that a real plan or a backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real one. I've watched the nurses for five years and I know the instruments already. Being a dental nurse still means holding the suction while a scared patient grips the chair, and a robot won't do that until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After 2031, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd have the flat and some savings, and I'd be 32. I'd figure it out then, I'm good at figuring it out.

say: I'd say **nobody's ready** for this, which is simply true.
I'd suggest at work that we **plan together**, and post useful advice rather than panic.
think: Even my **advantage goes** once AI handles rotas and insurers.
I'd have maybe **one year** before the owners notice.
do: Earn as much as possible from the **side business** in year one.
Start training as a **dental nurse** for the robot gap.
Rent out the **spare room** in her flat.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicked, steadied by her flat and savings.
S2.quote: Being a dental nurse still means holding the suction while a scared patient grips the chair, and a robot won't do that until 2031.
fieldNote: Rosa sees her **adaptability** stop being an advantage once AGI arrives.
She picks **dental nursing** because it's hands-on and she knows it.
She admits she **doesn't know** what comes after 2031.

steps.text: Sell AI admin set-ups to panicking practices in year one
Enrol in dental nurse training at Brightside's main clinic
Rent out the spare room in her flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so plan. At work I'd push the owners for a staff plan. I'd post about it practically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is good for me in the short run, as practice manager. But my job still ends by 2031. So I'd use those years to build something hands-on for after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the practice manager job and the pay rise in year one. I'd save hard, half of the pay rise. And in year two I'd start studying to be a dental hygienist, which is hands-on and better paid than nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control. It's a project, and I like projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hygienist training takes a while. Can you do it while managing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be tough, part-time over three years. Marco would have to do more at home, which he's said he would. Five years is enough to finish a hygienist course part-time if I start next September, and not one month later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your colleagues in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kerry and the others to start something now. Not to panic, just start. If they want, I'd help them find courses.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so plan.
I'd push the owners for a **staff plan** and post practical advice.
think: Five years is good **in the short run** as practice manager.
My job still **ends by 2031**, so I'd build something hands-on.
do: Get the **practice manager** job and raise in year one.
Start **hygienist training** part-time in year two.
feel: **Anxious but in control**, treating it like a project.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to finish a hygienist course part-time if I start next September, and not one month later.
fieldNote: Rosa plans a clear **two-stage** path: manager now, hygienist later.
She sets a **hard start date** to avoid drifting.
She'd encourage colleagues to **start now**, not panic.

steps.text: Take the practice manager job and its pay rise
Save half of the pay rise each month
Start part-time dental hygienist training next September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this well. At work I'd say let's plan it properly, and I'd help design it. Online I'd be positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd have years as practice manager, money saved, and time to train in something hands-on. I'd be 37, which is a nice age to start a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become practice manager in the first year and stay there for a good few years. I'd keep the side business going while it's useful. And in year three or four I'd train as a hygienist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of excitement. Ten years is long enough to have two careers, and I'd enjoy planning the second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you uneasy here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting too comfortable as manager, I suppose. And Marco's job, because kitchens might get robots around 2039 too. We'd have to plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money from the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put it towards a bigger flat, maybe, with a garden. Marco's always wanted a garden for herbs. It's a long-term thing.

I'd offer to help **design the plan** at work.
think: A decade gives me **years as manager**, savings and time to retrain.
At **37** I'd be at a nice age to start a second career.
do: Become **practice manager** in year one and stay a few years.
Keep the **side business** going while it's useful.
Train as a **hygienist** in year three or four.

S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to have two careers, and I'd enjoy planning the second one.
fieldNote: Rosa sees ten years as time for **two careers**.

steps.text: Take the practice manager role in year one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my main advantage, being quick with new tools, stops counting. What would help is cheaper, faster training for hands-on health jobs, so people can switch in months, not years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be on the winning side for a bit. Being the person who brings AI into the dental practice feels great until you realise you're also the one deciding who isn't needed.

headlineQuote: Being the person who brings AI into the dental practice feels great until you realise you're also the one deciding who isn't needed.
portrait: Rosa is a 27-year-old **dental group administrator** who runs three clinics from Harbour Road.
She uses AI **every day** and set up the practice's recall and claims tools.
Her **centre** outlook makes her practical: plan, train, don't panic.
She sees Steady Disruption as a **promotion**, but AGI removes her edge.
Her plan in the AGI pictures is **dental nursing or hygiene**, backed by an inherited flat.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being quick with new tools stops counting.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheaper, faster training** for hands-on health jobs.
